topic: The Dunning-Kruger effect explained in 50 seconds
title: Dunning-Kruger: What Everyone Gets Wrong
voiceover: Do clueless people really think they're geniuses? In 1999, David Dunning and Justin Kruger tested people on logic, grammar, and humor. Those who scored lowest still guessed they'd done better than average. The idea: the skills you need to do something well are the same skills you need to judge it. Importantly, their finding was about specific skills, not general intelligence. But here's the catch. Some statisticians argue part of that famous pattern is a statistical artifact, and the popular 'Mount Stupid' graph isn't actually from the paper. So don't use it to label other people. Use it on yourself: when you're new at something, ask an experienced person to rate your work. Tomorrow: why that annoying song is playing in your head right now.

description: Do unskilled people really think they're geniuses? Not quite. Dunning and Kruger found that low performers on specific tasks overestimated their performance, but the popular version of the story is oversimplified. Source: Kruger & Dunning (1999), 'Unskilled and unaware of it', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.
accuracy_note: Disputed/oversimplified: critics argue part of the classic pattern can arise from statistical effects (regression to the mean and the better-than-average effect). The popular 'Mount Stupid' curve does not appear in the original paper. The finding concerns specific skills, not general intelligence.
